chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Abdillah, from Mansur ibn al-Abbas, from al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Yaqtin, from Amr ibn Ibrahim, from Khalaf ibn Hammad, from Isma'il ibn Abi Qurrat, from Abi Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who borrowed one hundred dinars from another man and pledged jewelry to him as security for the one hundred dinars, then the borrower came to the lender and said, 'Lend me the security I pledged to you as a loan for use,' so he lent it to him, and the security perished in his possession. There is something due from the borrower to the lender in this matter. He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is upon the owner of the security (the borrower), for he is the one who pledged it and he is the one who caused its destruction, and there is no compensation for the property of this one (the lender).'
And Muhammad ibn Hassan narrated from Abu 'Imran al-Armani, from Abdillah ibn al-Hakam, who said

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who went bankrupt and had a debt owed to a group of people, and with some of them was security (pledged property) and with others there was no security, then he died and his wealth was not sufficient to cover the debt. He said: 'All that he left of the securities and other property is divided among the creditors in shares.'
And Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd narrated from Sulayman ibn Hafsh al-Marwazi, who said

I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) regarding a man who died with a debt and left nothing except a security in the hand of one of the creditors, and its price does not exceed more than the value of the security itself. Does he take it with its value, or is he and the other creditors partners in it? He wrote back (peace be upon him): 'All the creditors are equal in this; they distribute it among themselves in shares.'

And he said: And I wrote to him regarding a man who died and had heirs, and a man came and claimed a debt from him and said that he has a security with him. He wrote back (peace be upon him): 'If he has a debt from the deceased and has no proof against him, let him take his debt from what is in his hand and return the remainder to his heirs. And whenever he acknowledges what is in his hand, it is taken from him and he is required to provide proof for his claim, and he fulfills his right after the oath. And whenever he does not produce proof and the heirs deny, then he has an oath of knowledge upon them; they swear by Allah that they do not know that he has a right against their deceased.'
And Abu al-Husayn Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Asadi narrated from Musa ibn 'Imran al-Nakha'i, from his uncle Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Yazid al-Nawfali, from Ali ibn Salim, from his father, who said

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the report that was narrated: 'Whoever is more secure with a security than he is with his believing brother, then I am free from him.' He said: 'That is when the Right appears and our Qa'im, the Ahl al-Bayt (peace be upon him), rises.' I said: 'Then what is the report that was narrated:
And that the profit of a believer from a believer is usury?
He said: 'That is when the Right appears and our Qa'im, the Ahl al-Bayt (peace be upon him), rises. As for today, there is no harm if he sells to his believing brother and makes a profit on it.'

key_terms.أَهْلَ الْبَيْتِ: The People of the House (Ahl al-Bayt)
key_terms.رَهْن: Pledge or security (collateral) given for a debt

ai.seo_question: What are the Islamic legal rulings on pledged property (rahn) when a debtor goes bankrupt or dies?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between possession and liability in pledge (*rahn*) jurisprudence, establishing that the pledgor bears the risk of loss if the item is returned for use. It further codifies the principle of equal distribution among creditors in bankruptcy, ensuring that collateral held by individual lenders does not grant them priority over others. These rulings reflect the Imams' practical application of equity in commercial transactions, addressing common disputes in early Islamic society regarding debt recovery and asset liquidation.
